opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's a mixed picture. Animal models have been essential. They've taught us a huge amount about basic biology, and they're still an important safety check before anything goes into a person. But in terms of predicting whether a drug will actually work in humans, the track record isn't great. You'll often hear that something like nine out of ten drugs that look promising in preclinical studies fail once they reach clinical trials. A big part of that is that a mouse simply isn't a small human. The metabolism is different, the immune system is different, and the way a disease develops in an engineered mouse model often doesn't match how it develops in a real patient.

Cancer is a good example. We can cure cancer in mice over and over again, and very little of that translates. The tumors we implant or induce in animals don't capture the heterogeneity we see in people, or the way tumors evolve and respond to treatment over time.

So I don't think the answer is to throw animal testing out overnight. I think it's to be more thoughtful about when it's actually informative, and to complement it with better tools. That includes things like organoids and human tissue models, and increasingly computational approaches. We can use machine learning and mathematical modeling on human data, such as imaging, genomics, and clinical records, to get a better sense earlier on of who a drug might work for and why. If we can make better decisions before we ever get to an animal, or alongside it, we can hopefully reduce both the number of animals we use and the number of expensive late-stage failures.

r001.rationale: The response says roughly nine out of ten drugs that look promising in preclinical studies fail in clinical trials, conveying the stated high rate of failure to reproduce preclinical results in humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the honest answer is: not as well as most people assume, but better than nothing, and the gap between those two is where all the interesting problems live.

The number people usually cite is that something like nine out of ten drugs that look promising in animals fail once they get into human trials. A lot of that is efficacy, meaning the drug just doesn't do in people what it did in a mouse, and a chunk of it is toxicity we didn't see coming. So if you think of animal testing as a predictor, it's a pretty noisy one.

But I think the framing of "does it work" is a bit misleading. It works very well for some questions and poorly for others. If I want to know whether a compound is grossly toxic, whether it wrecks the liver or the kidneys at a high dose, animals are actually quite informative. Where it falls apart is in the subtle stuff, and especially in diseases where the animal model isn't really the disease. A mouse with an engineered tumor is not a person with a cancer that evolved over fifteen years in a body with its own immune system, its own metabolism, its own history. Same with Alzheimer's, same with a lot of psychiatric conditions. We've cured Alzheimer's in mice many, many times.

What I find more interesting is that the problem is partly biology and partly how we run the experiments. The animals are young, genetically identical, housed in sterile conditions, usually male. Patients are old, diverse, and sick with three other things. So some of the failure isn't that mice are bad proxies for humans, it's that we've designed the mouse studies in a way that strips out the variability we actually need to understand.

That's why I'm cautiously excited about the shift toward things like organoids and organ-on-a-chip systems, and about using patient data and computational models alongside animals rather than treating the animal study as the gate you pass through. I don't think we're at the point where you can drop animal work entirely, and I'd be skeptical of anyone who says we are. But I do think the question is changing from "can we replace animals" to "where exactly do animals add information, and where are we just doing it because that's how it's always been done."

r001.rationale: The response says roughly nine out of ten drugs that look promising in animals fail in human trials, explaining that many do not have the same efficacy in people.

astra-6.text: Animal testing can give us useful information about how a drug behaves in a living system, but it’s an imperfect predictor of what will happen in people. A treatment can look promising in animals and still turn out to be ineffective or unsafe in humans. So I think it has a role, but we need to be careful about how much confidence we place in those results and keep developing approaches that better reflect human biology.

r001.rationale: The response says animal results may fail to predict human outcomes, but does not state the roughly 80–90% failure rate.

So I think the question is where animal testing gives us useful evidence, and where human cells, tissue models, or computational approaches could give us better answers.
